title: Why micropayments need batching
text: A micropayment is a payment so small that the cost of moving it can exceed its value. Card networks charge a fixed fee per transaction, which is why nobody sells a single article for a tenth of a cent on that rail. Batching changes the arithmetic: thousands of tiny authorizations are collected, netted against one another and written to the ledger as one transaction, so the fixed cost is shared by everyone in the batch. The price of that efficiency is visibility. An individual payment is no longer a line on the public ledger, only a contribution to a net balance change, and anyone who wants a receipt has to ask the operator of the batch for it.

title: Citation is not attribution
text: When an assistant lists a source next to its answer, readers assume the answer was built from that source. That assumption is weak. A model can name a page it only skimmed, attach a link to a claim it produced from memory, or quote a sentence that the page never contained. Attribution that a reader can trust has to be checked mechanically: the quoted words must be found in the saved text of the source, and the answer must actually contain them. Anything less is a claim about provenance, and a claim is not the same thing as evidence that the words were used.

title: Spending limits for software agents
text: Software agents that pay for things need limits that they cannot talk their way around. A limit stored inside the agent is only a suggestion, because the agent can be misconfigured or manipulated. A limit enforced by the contract that moves the money is different: the owner of the funds chooses a maximum per task and a maximum per day, and the contract refuses any transfer beyond them. Such a mandate can be revoked at any time, and the funds stay in the owner's wallet until the moment they are spent, which removes the need to trust an intermediary with custody.
